title: Arrow prayers again
hook: short prayers fired through the day
tomorrow: why did her friends hold up coats instead of a speech?

segments.voice: Yesterday, work as prayer, and the line heartily, as to the Lord: the work itself, offered. Today, prayers short enough to fit inside the work.
screen: `HEARTILY, AS TO THE LORD.` → `PRAYERS THAT FIT INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Some prayers fill a page. This one fits in a single shout. A road out of Jericho, packed with people moving along with Jesus. At the edge of the crowd a blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits by the highway. He hears who's passing, and he starts to shout: “Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.” People turn around. Mark says “many charged him that he should hold his peace.” Be quiet. You're embarrassing everyone. And Bartimaeus…
screen: `ONE SHOUT, NOT A PAGE.` → `A BLIND MAN BY THE ROAD.` → `BE QUIET, SAYS THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: …shouts louder. Mark says “he cried the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me.” Jesus stands still and calls him. Bartimaeus throws off his coat, comes to Jesus, and asks to see. That's an arrow prayer: short, aimed, fired from wherever you are. Scripture has others. In one of Jesus' stories a tax collector stands far off at the temple and says only: “God be merciful to me a sinner.” Jesus says that man went home justified. A psalm gives another: “Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD.” John Cassian wrote that monks of the Egyptian desert carried that line through the whole day: waking, working, tempted, bored. Arrow prayers again, because the path has met them before. This time they go inside a whole day. Paul's “Pray without ceasing” sounds impossible beside a calendar; nobody can kneel all day. But a short line can ride along in the cracks: the waiting room, the walk to the car, the second before answering the phone. Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, which echoes Bartimaeus: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Short. Again. All day.
screen: `HE CRIED THE MORE.` · `GOD BE MERCIFUL TO ME.` · `MAKE HASTE TO HELP ME.` · `SHORT LINES IN THE CRACKS.` · then, large: `ALL DAY, SHORT.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for a minute, around a room or down a hall. Choose one short line, have mercy on me, make haste to help me, or simply thanks, and let it come once every few steps. Then sit for what's left of the time and let the line go quiet.
Arrow prayers again. Short prayers fired through the day, like Bartimaeus shouting from the side of the road.
Your line: all day, short. Bartimaeus needed one sentence, and he wasn't hushed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray short lines through the day, such as Lord, have mercy, a line from a psalm, or the Jesus Prayer, often silently and in the middle of other things.

fork.setup: a coworker says pray without ceasing is impossible with a full-time job. what does the lesson answer?
options: right; it was only ever meant for monks in the desert.
short lines in the cracks: the walk, the wait, the second before a call.

fork.reveal: Cassian's desert monks carried one short psalm line through work and rest. pray without ceasing becomes many short prayers.

options: You don't need a whole one. One short line, again and again, like Bartimaeus.
Wait until you're calm enough to pray properly, then pray at length.

chat.meaning: Bartimaeus shouted one short line, and cried it again when hushed. Arrow prayers fit the cracks of a day, even a waiting room.

Bartimaeus.meaning: a blind beggar near Jericho who called out to Jesus

Jericho.meaning: an ancient town near the Jordan River

John Cassian.meaning: an early monk who wrote down the desert monks' teaching

Jesus Prayer.meaning: a short Orthodox prayer asking Jesus for mercy
